newsitem.title: USA: Heating oil, coffee, pork bellies rise, wheat falls.
newsitem.headline: Heating oil, coffee, pork bellies rise, wheat falls.

text.p: Heating oil prices rose on Wednesday after a sharp reduction in stockpiles was reported, while coffee prices advanced as roasters returned to the market to secure supplies.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, heating oil for May delivery closed 0.82 cent a gallon higher at 55.65 cents.

"The market was teetering all day, but it was buying in heating oil which held everything together at the end after its more-bullish-than-expected stock decline," said Tim Evans, analyst with Pegasus Econometric Group.

On Tuesday evening, the American Petroleum Institute in its weekly report said U.S. stockpiles of distillate, which comprises heating oil and diesel, fell by a sharp 4.7 million barrels in the week ended April 18 to 96.3 million barrels.

Traders had been expecting a drop of 500,000 to 2 million barrels. The surprising size of the drop confirmed that weeks of unseasonably cold weather in the U.S. Northeast had begun to drain refiners of heating oil supplies.
Last week Sun Co had said it was left without any heating oil for distributors until later this week.
Buoyed by the gain in heating oil, crude oil for May delivery ended 14 cents a barrel higher at $19.73.

But gasoline prices fell after the API said gasoline production rose to 7.7 million barrels a day last week, up from 7.4 million a week earlier and a level that dealers said should make supplies ample for the summer driving season.
May unleaded gasoline closed at 61.74 cents a gallon, down 0.03 cent.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee prices rose as roasters joined speculators in buying futures contracts amid worries about available supplies from South America.
Coffee for May delivery closed 3.10 cents a pound higher at 214.30 cents.

News that negotiations aimed at resolving a truckers' strike in Colombia had reached a stalemate provided some impetus, but traders said the reappearance of steady roaster buying was even more significant today.

With arabica or "mild" South American coffee inventories already near historically low levels in the United States, a prolonged work stoppage in Colombia, the world's number two grower, could drive futures sharply higher, traders said.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, pork belly futures rose to new life-of-contract highs on signs of buoyant demand from domestic bacon slicers and booming exports to fill the void left by Taiwan's sudden halt in pork exports last month.
Pork bellies for May delivery closed at 92.125 cents a pound, up 2.30 cents.

Prices rose from the start after Tuesday night's weekly report on pork belly stocks, which showed 409,000 pounds of bellies moved out of exchange-approved warehouses outside the Chicago area. Analysts had expected a small net in-movement.
"If we're not storing now, there's not going to be anything for the summer" when demand for bacon peaks, said Julia Bussie, analyst for AG Edwards. "We're pricing out domestic demand," Bussie added.

Traders also noted a slowdown in the pace of hog slaughter in the Midwest and signs that the epidemic of foot-and-mouth disease in Taiwan's hog herd may be spreading. Taiwan was the world's number two pork exporter last year after Denmark.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat prices fell back as forecasts for rain in parched European wheat areas later this week eased some worries about world supplies later this year.
Wheat for May delivery closed 9-1/2 cents a bushel lower at $4.32-1/4.
"There's a forecast for rain in France Friday, Sunday and Monday and that's taking us down," said Steve Bruce of E.D. and F. Man International.

The National Meteorological Service Meteo France said light rains were expected in western France by Friday and more substantial rains may fall over the weekend. Dry weather in France, Europe's top grower, has trimmed production prospects.
Traders also cited a feeling that damage estimates to winter wheat hit by a freeze in the High Plains from Kansas to Texas last week had been overdone.
